clips.text: Your body was never built to drink milk.
clips.image: ACTION/AFTERMATH: a Neolithic herder in a rough wool tunic doubled over clutching his stomach in pain beside a spilled clay cup of milk on the grass, goats watching behind him, warm pasture cream morning light, fresh meadow green fields, high contrast, cinematic, no text
clips.note: AUTOPSY: hook sentence 1 ONLY (~3.5s); ACTION/AFTERMATH image (doubled over, spilled cup), face visible, high contrast; aggressive zoom-punch; 350ms pause after a1; bed in after this sentence

clips.text: Seventy percent of the world still can't drink it.
clips.image: PAYOFF FLASH (fresh image, NOT a diagram crop): extreme close-up of a glowing DNA double helix in warm cream light, one single letter glowing bright meadow green and flipping over, deep green background, dramatic, no text
clips.note: AUTOPSY: payoff flash lands ~4s (a genuinely DIFFERENT dramatic image from a1); this IS the twist visual — c7 reuses this exact asset; count-up pop '70'

clips.text: Next: the cheese trick, the one-letter mutation, the seven-thousand-year-old strainers — and your turn.
clips.image: Split triptych feel in one frame: a clay pot of cheese curds, a glowing DNA letter, an ancient pierced pottery strainer, warm pasture cream morning light, fresh meadow green fields, fresh meadow green background, warm cream accents, no text
clips.note: AUTOPSY: re-orientation TIGHT — 15 words, ~6s spoken (<= ~8s); music fades in ONLY after a1's first spoken sentence

clips.text: It starts about eight thousand five hundred years ago, in the Fertile Crescent, where the first farmers are learning to milk a goat. A man lifts a clay cup to his mouth and drinks — and an hour later, his stomach turns inside out. He has done nothing wrong. His body simply cannot do what the cup is asking. He tries again the next morning, and the next — because the cup is food, and food is survival.
clips.image: a Neolithic herder in a rough wool tunic lifting a clay cup of fresh milk to his mouth at sunrise in a meadow pasture, goats grazing behind him, warm pasture cream morning light, fresh meadow green fields, photorealistic, no text
clips.note: open loop 1 (mini): tease overlay + push-in

clips.text: Here is the problem, plainly. Milk is full of a sugar called lactose. To digest it, you need an enzyme called lactase — and babies make plenty of it. But after childhood, for most humans in history, the lactase tap simply switched off.
clips.image: A close-up of a clay cup of milk on a wooden table at sunrise, a small glass vial of golden enzyme beside it, a baby goat drinking from its mother in the background, warm pasture cream morning light, fresh meadow green fields, photorealistic, no text

clips.text: Picture a room of ten adults, eight thousand five hundred years ago. Seven of them drink a cup of fresh milk — and seven of them spend the afternoon doubled over. That is not bad luck. That is the default setting of the human body.
clips.image: Ten Neolithic villagers in a meadow settlement at sunrise, seven of them clutching their stomachs in discomfort while three stand fine holding clay cups, warm pasture cream morning light, fresh meadow green fields, photorealistic, no text
clips.note: rule 15: 7-of-10 visualised as a room of ten people

clips.text: So how did milk go from poison to the most ordinary drink on Earth? The answer starts with a trick — not in the body, but in a pot. That is the cheese.
clips.image: A clay pot on a wooden table at sunrise, white cheese curds inside it, a wooden spoon resting on the rim, morning light across the table, warm pasture cream morning light, fresh meadow green fields, photorealistic, no text
clips.note: chapter-end open loop 2: tease overlay + push-in + 1s riser

clips.text: Chapter two: the cheese trick. Before anyone could drink milk, someone had to outsmart it.
clips.image: A Neolithic kitchen at sunrise, a woman stirring a clay pot of curdling milk over a small fire, cheese cloths hanging behind her, warm pasture cream morning light, fresh meadow green fields, photorealistic, no text
clips.note: chapter card

clips.text: The first clue is on the pots. On broken pottery from the Fertile Crescent, chemists found the fatty fingerprints of milk — eight thousand five hundred years old. People were milking animals long before anyone could digest what came out.
clips.image: A close-up of an ancient broken pottery shard on a wooden table, a scientist's gloved hand holding it under a lamp, faint golden fat residue glowing on the clay, warm pasture cream morning light, fresh meadow green fields, photorealistic, no text

clips.text: Then, in Poland, archaeologists found something stranger: pottery full of tiny holes, seven thousand years old. They were strainers — sieves for separating curds from whey. The oldest cheesemaking kit on Earth.
clips.image: An archaeologist's hands holding a piece of ancient pierced pottery full of tiny holes, white curds visible through the holes, a dig site in Poland behind, morning light, photorealistic, no text
clips.note: real evidence: Bogucki 1970s, Kujawy Poland; Roffet-Salque 2011 milk fats

clips.text: Here is why it worked. Fermentation eats the lactose. Turn milk into cheese or yogurt, and the sugar that made you sick mostly disappears. The herders had hacked milk — a thousand years before anyone's body could handle the fresh stuff.
clips.image: A clay bowl of fresh white yogurt beside a wedge of hard cheese on a wooden table at sunrise, a goat watching from the doorway, warm pasture cream morning light, fresh meadow green fields, photorealistic, no text
clips.note: keyword pop 'THE CHEESE TRICK'

clips.text: Think about what that means. For a thousand years, dairy was cheese, not milk. No one drank a fresh glass, because no one could. The cup stayed on the shelf — while the cheese went on the table.
clips.image: A wooden shelf in a Neolithic hut at sunrise, clay cups standing untouched in a row, a round of cheese on the table below being cut with a stone knife, warm pasture cream morning light, fresh meadow green fields, photorealistic, no text

clips.text: But cheese has a limit. It is slow, it is work, and it never gives you the fresh milk itself. And then, about seven thousand five hundred years ago, in the plains of central Europe — one letter in the code changed.
clips.image: A wide shot of the central European plains at sunrise, a Neolithic farming village with cattle and goats in the meadow, a single letter glowing faintly green in the sky above, warm pasture cream morning light, fresh meadow green fields, photorealistic, no text

clips.text: A single letter. C becomes T. And suddenly, the tap that was supposed to switch off at age seven… stays on. That is the letter.
clips.image: Extreme close-up of a glowing DNA strand at sunrise, one single letter changing from C to T in bright meadow green light, cream background, dramatic, no text
clips.note: chapter-end open loop 3: tease overlay + push-in + 1s riser; keyword pop 'ONE LETTER'

clips.text: Chapter three: the letter. Your lactase gene has a switch next to it — and seven thousand five hundred years ago, that switch broke in the on position.
clips.image: A glowing DNA double helix at sunrise, a small switch beside it flipped to the on position and glowing green, cream background, scientific illustration style, no text
clips.note: chapter card

clips.text: Every baby is born with the enzyme switched on. Milk is a baby's only food, so the body makes lactase in abundance. Then, around age seven or eight, the switch flips off — in most mammals, and in most humans, forever.
clips.image: A Neolithic mother nursing her baby at sunrise in a meadow hut, a clay cup of milk standing untouched on the table beside them, warm pasture cream morning light, fresh meadow green fields, photorealistic, no text
clips.note: keyword pop 'SWITCHED OFF'

clips.text: The change is almost absurdly small. One letter in the DNA near the lactase gene — a C becomes a T. It does not build anything new. It simply stops the switch from flipping off. And the enzyme keeps flowing, for life.
clips.image: A close-up of a DNA strand with one single glowing letter highlighted in bright meadow green among ordinary grey letters, cream background, scientific illustration style, no text
clips.note: uncertainty boundary: the European -13910 C-to-T is the best studied; other independent mutations exist

clips.text: The mechanism has four moves. First: the gene. The lactase gene sits on chromosome two, waiting for orders — and the orders come from a switch just beside it.
clips.image: ONE gene-switch asset, full view: a human chromosome pair with a glowing lactase gene, a small switch beside it, and a flowing enzyme stream below, deep meadow green background, warm cream light, scientific illustration style, NO text, NO labels, NO letters
clips.note: dataScene beat 1 of 4: staged reveal, one asset; c5-c7 are true crops of this

clips.text: Second: the switch. In most of us, the switch flips off after childhood. In the mutants — and I mean that as a compliment — the switch is jammed on.
clips.image: TRUE CROP of the c4 gene-switch asset, zoomed into the switch zone: a small switch jammed in the on position glowing bright green, no text
clips.note: dataScene beat 2: true crop of c4 asset

clips.text: Third: the enzyme. With the switch stuck on, lactase keeps breaking lactose into glucose and galactose — the two simple sugars your gut can actually absorb.
clips.image: TRUE CROP of the c4 gene-switch asset, zoomed into the enzyme stream zone: golden enzyme molecules breaking apart sugar crystals, no text
clips.note: dataScene beat 3: true crop of c4 asset

clips.text: Fourth: the takeover. The people with the switch on had food when crops failed, and water when wells ran dry. Models suggest they had up to nineteen percent more children — and that edge, compounded over centuries, took over a continent.
clips.image: PAYOFF FLASH asset reused (a2): extreme close-up of a glowing DNA double helix in warm cream light, one single letter glowing bright meadow green and flipping over, deep green background, dramatic, no text
clips.note: dataScene beat 4 = TWIST; reuses the a2 image (NOT a crop of c4 — see Known deviations); chapter-end open loop 4

clips.text: Culture rewrote the genome — and the proof is on a map. Where your family comes from decides, almost exactly, whether milk loves you back. That is the map.
clips.image: A Neolithic herder standing on a green hill at sunrise looking out over a wide plain, a faint glowing map of Europe in the sky above him, warm pasture cream morning light, fresh meadow green fields, photorealistic, no text
clips.note: differentiator stated plainly: we started drinking it, and evolution followed

clips.text: Chapter four: the map. Today, about thirty-five percent of the world can drink milk as adults. The other sixty-five percent cannot — and the line between them is drawn by ancestry. Draw that line on a map, and you can read seven thousand years of history in it.
clips.image: A world map painted on an old parchment at sunrise, northern Europe glowing bright green and East Asia dim, a clay cup of milk resting on the map, warm pasture cream morning light, fresh meadow green fields, photorealistic, no text
clips.note: chapter card; count-up pop '35' lands on d6, not here

clips.text: The record has five marks. First: eleven thousand years ago, in the Middle East, people domesticate cattle, goats, and sheep — for meat, not milk.
clips.image: ONE timeline asset, full view: a horizontal timeline from 11,000 years ago to today on a deep meadow green background, five glowing cream milestones rising along it, a small clay cup motif at each milestone, scientific diagram style, NO text, NO labels, NO letters
clips.note: dataScene beat 1 of 5: staged reveal, one asset; d3-d6 are true crops of this

clips.text: Second: eight thousand five hundred years ago, milk fat appears on pots in the Fertile Crescent. The milking has begun — but the drinking has not.
clips.image: TRUE CROP of the d2 timeline asset, zoomed into the second milestone zone: a glowing cream milestone with a small pottery shard motif, no text
clips.note: dataScene beat 2: true crop of d2 asset

clips.text: Third: seven thousand five hundred years ago, the letter flips in central Europe. The switch stays on — and the farmers who carry it start to spread.
clips.image: TRUE CROP of the d2 timeline asset, zoomed into the third milestone zone: a glowing cream milestone with a small DNA letter motif, no text
clips.note: dataScene beat 3: true crop of d2 asset

clips.text: Fourth: seven thousand years ago, in Poland, the cheese strainers. The hack is now a craft — and dairy is spreading across a continent.
clips.image: TRUE CROP of the d2 timeline asset, zoomed into the fourth milestone zone: a glowing cream milestone with a small pierced strainer motif, no text
clips.note: dataScene beat 4: true crop of d2 asset

clips.text: Fifth: today. Thirty-five percent of the world keeps the enzyme for life — about ninety percent in northern Europe, as low as five percent in parts of East Asia. One letter, two worlds.
clips.image: TRUE CROP of the d2 timeline asset, zoomed into the whole-timeline zone: all five glowing cream milestones along the timeline, a rising sun glowing above the last one, no text
clips.note: dataScene beat 5; count-up pop '35'

clips.text: And there is a wrinkle the textbooks argue about. In Africa, herders were drinking milk thousands of years before the mutation arrived — we know from milk proteins on their teeth. They drank it fermented, and they drank it anyway, symptoms and all.
clips.image: African herders with their cattle at sunrise on a dry golden savanna, clay pots of fermented milk beside them, warm pasture cream morning light, fresh meadow green fields, photorealistic, no text
clips.note: uncertainty boundary: teeth proteins prove milk was consumed, not that it was tolerated

clips.text: There is one more reason the letter spread: drought. In a dry year, a cow is a walking well — milk is water you can carry, food you can drink, and it never needs a river.
clips.image: A cow standing by a dry cracked riverbed at sunrise, a Neolithic herder milking it into a clay cup, golden dry grass all around, warm pasture cream morning light, fresh meadow green fields, photorealistic, no text
clips.note: spread hypothesis: famine insurance / clean water in drought (debated — presented as a reason, not a proven cause)

clips.text: So the map is drawn. The question is where YOU stand on it — and there is a test, a glass of milk, and twenty-four hours. That is the test.
clips.image: a Neolithic herder in a rough wool tunic holding up a full clay cup of milk toward the camera at sunrise, his expression daring you to drink it, goats behind him, warm pasture cream morning light, fresh meadow green fields, photorealistic, no text
clips.note: chapter-end open loop 5: tease overlay + push-in + 1s riser

clips.text: Chapter five: the test. You have heard the poison, the cheese, the letter, and the map. Now the choice — and the glass — is yours.
clips.image: A full glass of fresh milk on a wooden table at sunrise, a Neolithic herder's hand reaching for it, morning light through the window, warm pasture cream morning light, fresh meadow green fields, photorealistic, no text
clips.note: chapter card

clips.text: Here is the test, from a real gut doctor: drink a large glass of milk, then wait twenty-four hours. Bloated? Gurgling? Running for the bathroom? Then your switch flipped off, like most of the world.
clips.image: A modern person in a kitchen at sunrise drinking a large glass of milk, a wall clock behind them showing the hours passing, warm morning light, photorealistic, no text
clips.note: self-test from Dr. Miranda Lomer (Guy's and St Thomas')

clips.text: But here is the catch. Intolerance is not an allergy. Many people who fail the glass test can still drink milk in tea, or on cereal — a little at a time, the gut copes. A splash in tea is about fifty millilitres; a bowl of cereal, two hundred and fifty to three hundred and seventy-five — small doses, spread out, and the gut copes. It is a dimmer, not a wall.
clips.image: A cup of tea with a splash of milk beside a bowl of cereal with milk at sunrise on a kitchen table, a small measuring jug nearby, warm morning light, photorealistic, no text

clips.text: And a second catch: the test is not really about milk. It is about where your ancestors lived. Northern Europe, parts of Africa, the Middle East, South Asia — the map of milk is the map of herders.
clips.image: Four herders from four different lands standing together at sunrise — northern Europe, Africa, the Middle East, South Asia — each holding a clay cup of milk, warm pasture cream morning light, fresh meadow green fields, photorealistic, no text

clips.text: So here is the question the story turns on: is milk a superfood — or a poison your ancestors never signed up for?
clips.image: a Neolithic herder in a rough wool tunic alone on a green hill at sunrise, looking out over a valley of farms and herds under a cream sky, thoughtful, warm pasture cream morning light, fresh meadow green fields, photorealistic, no text
clips.note: RHETORICAL-QUESTION beat: slower drift + music duck; 1.75s full silence after (gap)

clips.text: There is no right answer. There is only the answer your DNA gives — and it was written seven thousand five hundred years ago. Which brings us to today. That is the choice.
clips.image: a Neolithic herder in a rough wool tunic walking toward the camera at sunrise, a clay cup in his hand, meadow green fields behind him, cream morning light, photorealistic, no text
clips.note: chapter-end open loop 6: tease overlay + push-in + 1s riser

clips.text: One last thing about the test: if you pass it, thank a farmer from seven thousand years ago. If you fail it, you are in the majority — seventy percent of humanity is on your side.
clips.image: A Neolithic farming family at sunrise sharing a meal in a meadow, clay cups of milk raised together, goats grazing nearby, warm pasture cream morning light, fresh meadow green fields, photorealistic, no text

clips.text: Chapter six: today. You still drink milk from a carton, still hear the word superfood. Nothing about the milk has changed — except now you know what it cost to earn it.
clips.image: A modern kitchen at sunrise, a carton of milk on the counter beside a glass, a Neolithic clay cup standing next to it like a museum piece, warm morning light, photorealistic, no text
clips.note: chapter card

clips.text: Remember the numbers: seventy percent of the world still can't, thirty-five percent can, one letter flipped seven thousand five hundred years ago, and the carriers had up to nineteen percent more children.
clips.image: A glass of milk on a windowsill at sunrise beside a coiled glowing green thread, a dark room, warm cream light, photorealistic, no text
clips.note: rule 15: numbers visualised; 'about' per uncertainty boundary; keyword pop 'SEVENTY PERCENT'

clips.text: And remember the twist: the enemy was never the milk. It was a switch that flipped off at age seven — until one letter jammed it on, and a poison became a pantry.
clips.image: A pantry shelf at sunrise, clay pots of cheese and yogurt lined up beside a full clay cup of fresh milk, a green glow behind the cup, warm pasture cream morning light, fresh meadow green fields, photorealistic, no text
clips.note: keyword pop 'POISON TO PANTRY'; differentiator stated plainly

clips.text: Can you drink a full glass of milk on an empty stomach — or does your body say no? Tell us what happens, and where in the world your family comes from.
clips.image: a Neolithic herder in a rough wool tunic looking straight at camera, a full clay cup of milk in his hand, meadow green fields behind him, warm cream morning light, photorealistic, no text
clips.note: COMMENT QUESTION (locked, verbatim): 1.5s VO pause + deeper bed duck after

clips.text: Science note, plainly: seven thousand five hundred years is a model estimate, not a dated fossil; seventy and thirty-five percent are population averages that swing wildly by ancestry; the nineteen-percent figure is a model, not a count; and milk was never poison in the lethal sense — it made people sick, and this note says so.
clips.image: Calm deep meadow green panorama with a single glowing cream thread stretched across an empty pasture at sunrise, vast and peaceful, photorealistic, no text
clips.note: uncertainty recap, explicit

clips.text: The named sources, so you can check me: the Nature milk revolution of 2013; Mélanie Roffet-Salque's cheese strainers from Poland; and the lactase persistence studies of Itan, Enattah, and Tishkoff.
clips.image: A lab notebook and a clay cheese strainer on a desk, a glowing green thread across the pages, warm lamp light, photorealistic, no text
clips.note: rule 24: named sources in VO

clips.text: Your body was never built to drink milk. The next time you lift a glass without thinking, you will not even notice. Now you know what that freedom is worth.
clips.image: a Neolithic herder in a rough wool tunic walking away along a meadow path at sunrise, his shadow long in the cream light, goats following behind, cinematic wide shot, photorealistic, no text
clips.note: closing line; logical loop back to the opening hook

clips.text: Milk was poison — until one letter made it a pantry. Goodnight. And if milk ever makes you sick — blame the switch, not the cow.
clips.image: A sunrise over a quiet pasture, cream light breaking over green hills, a cow grazing peacefully in the foreground, cinematic wide shot, photorealistic, no text
clips.note: closing echo of the title
